Gravity: TreePM (Barnes-Hut oct-tree short-range + PM long-range, FFT)
Neighbour_structure: Same BH oct-tree used as a range-search tree for SPH neighbours
Multipole: Monopole only (deliberate regression from GADGET-1 octopoles)
Leaf_bucket: Tree walked to individual particles; Peano-Hilbert ordered
Why: Oct-tree is shallower than a binary k-d tree (~0.3-0.65 N internal nodes vs ~N), bounded node aspect ratio keeps high-order multipoles small, and the same tree does double duty as the SPH range-search structure; monopoles give a memory-efficient build and cheap dynamic updates

Gravity: One-sided TreePM OR manifestly momentum-conserving FMM
Neighbour_structure: Oct-tree with Peano-Hilbert ordering; hierarchical particle groups
Multipole: FMM with symmetric cell-cell expansions (momentum conserving by construction)
Why: FMM restores exact momentum conservation that one-sided tree walks break, and gives better force accuracy per interaction at high dynamic range (zoom runs with extreme density contrast)

Gravity: Fast Multipole Method, 4th-order moments stored, 5th-order local expansion; 5th-order Ewald for periodic images
Neighbour_structure: Balanced binary k-d tree, hierarchically sorted particles
Multipole: 4th order (hexadecapole) stored; local expansion to 5th order
Leaf_bucket: bucket b~16 particles; traversal group g=64 (=4b)
Published_performance: 3.8 million particles/s/node at N=1e12 (Titan, 1 K20X GPU per node); cf. HACC 1.7 and 2HOT 1.2 on the same problem size; force errors ~1e-5 relative (single-precision interactions accumulated in double)
Why: FMM errors are spatially less correlated than Barnes-Hut errors; 4th-order moments are >2x more efficient than quadrupoles once you need <0.1% RMS force error; large buckets/groups produce long interaction lists that saturate a GPU
Reference: Potter, Stadel & Teyssier 2017, Comput. Astrophys. Cosmol. 4,2, doi:10.1186/s40668-017-0021-1 (arXiv:1609.08621)

Gravity: Barnes-Hut tree on space-filling-curve keys, Charm++ over-decomposition
Neighbour_structure: Same tree; SPH neighbour search via tree range query
Leaf_bucket: Configurable bucket; tree pieces sized for load balance
Published_performance: Strong scaling to 512k cores of Blue Waters at 12-24e9 particles; clustered datasets to 128k cores
Why: Charm++ message-driven execution hides communication latency and lets a highly clustered (high dynamic range) dataset be load-balanced by migrating tree pieces rather than by geometric bisection
Reference: Menon et al. 2015, Comput. Astrophys. Cosmol. 2,1, doi:10.1186/s40668-015-0007-9 (arXiv:1409.1929)

Gravity: Sparse Barnes-Hut oct-tree, entirely GPU-resident; Barnes (1994)-style group MAC
Neighbour_structure: Morton-key sort + parallel-scan octree build (no CPU involvement)
Leaf_bucket: Particle groups traversed together (shared interaction list)
Published_performance: 2.8e6 particles/s at theta=0.75, N=1e6, one GTX480 (1.345 TF peak FP32); 2.1e6/s on Tesla C2050; ~1 GB device memory per 5e6 particles. Galaxy merger (240,002 bodies): max energy error 2.8e-4 at theta=0.75 vs 1.3e-4 at theta=0.50, costing 7102 s vs 12687 s. Later: 24.77 Pflops sustained, 242e9 particles, 18600 GPUs on Titan
Why: Keeping tree build AND traverse on the GPU removes the PCIe round trip that dominated earlier GPU tree codes; parallel-scan/sort primitives make it portable to any device with those primitives (explicitly noted as OpenCL-portable)
Reference: Bedorf, Gaburov & Portegies Zwart 2012, J. Comput. Phys. 231,2825, doi:10.1016/j.jcp.2011.12.024 (arXiv:1106.1900); Bedorf et al. 2014, arXiv:1412.0659

Neighbour_structure: Tree range search; meshless finite-volume/-mass partition of unity for hydro
Why: Reuses a proven gravity solver and changes the hydro discretisation; the neighbour structure has to support a smoothly varying kernel support radius, which a tree does naturally and a uniform grid does not

Neighbour_structure: Moving Voronoi tessellation (Delaunay) for hydro; oct-tree for gravity and for mesh-construction searches
Why: A Voronoi mesh is the natural adaptive neighbour structure when you want Galilean-invariant finite-volume hydro; the tessellation itself supplies neighbours with no capacity parameter at all

Gravity: Fast Multipole Method (default order p=4, compile-time selectable up to p=5), optionally + PM for periodic volumes
Neighbour_structure: Hierarchical cell grid, task-based; leaf cells hold many particles; pair tasks enumerated once per rebuild
Leaf_bucket: Large leaf cells (many particles) so multipole storage is amortised
GPU: No (task-based CPU; GPU work in progress)
Why: FMM lists all interactions explicitly so the whole step becomes a task graph with no decision-making during traversal; large leaves make P2P kernels vectorise; MAC follows Salmon & Warren (1994) error analysis rather than a bare opening angle

Gravity: Exact near/far split: direct 1/r^2 for the near field, discrete multipole convolution on a STATIC mesh for the far field
Neighbour_structure: Static cell decomposition (cells sized so the near-field radius is a small integer number of cells)
Multipole: High-order multipoles on the static mesh
Published_performance: 70e6 particle updates/s/node on Summit (6x V100/node -> ~1.2e7/s/GPU by my division); median fractional force error 1e-5
Why: A static mesh makes the far-field operator a fixed convolution computed once, so the only per-step work is the near-field direct sum - which is exactly the operation GPUs are best at; the analytic near/far separation makes the force error controlled and homogeneous

Neighbour_structure: Oct-tree + PM mesh; recursive multi-section domain decomposition
Published_performance: 5e4 particles/s/CPU core at theta=0.5 on Cray XT4 when >1e6 particles/core; load-imbalance loss ~4% beyond 1e3 cores
Why: TreePM confines the tree to a short range so tree depth (and therefore the cost of extreme density contrast) is bounded, while the PM part carries the long-range force at fixed O(N + M^3 log M) cost

Gravity: Long-range spectral PM + short-range solver that is P3M or TreePM depending on architecture
Neighbour_structure: Chaining mesh / tree for the short range
Published_performance: 1.7e6 particles/s/node at N=1e12 (as quoted by Potter et al. 2017)
Why: Deliberately splits the algorithm so the long-range part is architecture-independent and only the short-range kernel is re-written per machine
Reference: Habib et al. 2015, New Astron. 42,49, doi:10.1016/j.newast.2015.06.003 (arXiv:1410.2805)

Neighbour_structure: Hashed oct-tree keyed on Morton/Hilbert index - a spatial hash whose keys ENCODE tree level, so capacity is never fixed
Multipole: High order with explicit error analysis
Published_performance: 1.2e6 particles/s/node at N=1e12 (as quoted by Potter et al. 2017); >10 runs of 4096^3 particles
Why: Hashing tree cells (rather than space) gives O(1) cell lookup with full adaptivity; the same key structure drives the domain decomposition
Reference: Warren 2013, arXiv:1310.4502; original: Warren & Salmon 1993, doi:10.1145/169627.169640

Gravity: k-d tree, Cartesian multipoles, long-range force evaluated ONCE PER LEAF NODE and Taylor-expanded to the particles
Neighbour_structure: Same k-d tree, built by recursive bisection of the longest axis; one neighbour search per leaf node
Published_performance: No GPU rate; low-memory design is the stated goal
Why: One tree serves both SPH neighbour finding and gravity, which is what makes softening = smoothing length enforceable; per-leaf evaluation amortises the tree walk over ~10 particles. The neighbour cache is a memory-locality optimisation only - the full trial neighbour list is always kept, positions beyond the cache are re-read from memory

Gravity: Particle-mesh on an adaptive (octree) mesh, multigrid/relaxation Poisson solve
Neighbour_structure: AMR octree of grids; refinement triggered on particle count per cell
Leaf_bucket: Refine when a cell exceeds a particle-count threshold
Why: Refining the MESH on density is the direct structural answer to unbounded density contrast: the grid follows the matter instead of the matter overflowing the grid
Structured patches give cache-friendly stencils; refinement criteria are physics-driven (overdensity, Jeans length) rather than capacity-driven

Gravity: Direct summation with the Ahmad-Cohen neighbour scheme: irregular (near) force on CPU/SIMD, regular (far) force on GPU; KS/chain regularisation for close pairs
Neighbour_structure: Per-particle neighbour LIST with an adaptive radius, rebuilt on the regular-force cadence
Published_performance: Million-body globular cluster with 5% primordial binaries: ~1 h per half-mass crossing time on 320 CPU cores + 32 K20X GPUs; 400-2000x faster than NBODY6
Why: Collisional stellar dynamics (binaries, mass segregation, BH dynamics) requires exact forces; the regular force involves ~99% of the particles but is updated ~20x less often than the irregular force, which is where the saving comes from
